title: Both Ends of the Earth: the Passages, the Pole, and the Sea With No Grave
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Borge, Ostfold: the fourth son of a shipping house
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth date and parentage from Britannica and the MiA/Roald Amundsen's House person records; the pin is the Tomta site on the Hvidsten farm land at Borge, between Fredrikstad and Sarpsborg, given to two decimals only. The family's move to Kristiania is undated in the reachable sources and is carried inside this campa rather than given a stop of its own.
stops.campa: In the shipping country between Fredrikstad and Sarpsborg, on the Hvidsten farm land at Borge, a fourth son is born to the shipowner and master mariner Jens Engebreth Amundsen and to Hanne Henrikke Gustava Sahlqvist. The house is full of sea: ships owned, ships commanded, ships lost with their crews. The family moves up to Kristiania while he is still small and he grows up in the Uranienborg streets, where one of the neighbourhood boys is Carsten Borchgrevink, who will land in Antarctica before him. His mother intends him for medicine.
suggested_refs: The Tomta site at Hvidsten, Borge, and the MiA person record for Jens Engebreth Amundsen

stops.name: Kristiansand: the father dies aboard the Rollo
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Fram Museum chronology; MiA person record for Jens Engebreth Amundsen); month and day not established in this pass and defaulted to 01. The pin is Kristiansand harbour; the death was at sea off the town and has no fixed position.
stops.campa: The steamship Rollo comes down from England carrying Jens Engebreth Amundsen, shipowner and master mariner, and off Kristiansand the old captain dies aboard her, homeward bound. His son Roald is fourteen. The shipping towns of that coast lose men at sea most years, and this family absorbs it as the others do. The boy stays where his mother has put him, at school, on the road to a profession ashore. He does not go to sea himself for another seven years.
suggested_refs: The MiA person record for Jens Engebreth Amundsen, shipowner and master mariner
sources: Roald Amundsen's House / MiA, person record for Jens Engebreth Amundsen

stops.name: Royal Frederick University, Kristiania: the medicine he does not finish
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1890-1893 (Fram Museum chronology; Britannica; Wikipedia). Month of enrolment not fixed and defaulted to 01. The mother's death and the signing-on aboard the sealer Magdalena, both 1893, are carried in this campa and have no separate stop, the Magdalena's port of departure not being established in this pass.
stops.campa: At his mother's wish he enrols in medicine, and by every account he is an indifferent student. The energy goes elsewhere: skiing, long marches in winter, and the literature of Sir John Franklin's lost expedition, which he later says decided the course of his life. In 1893 Hanne Henrikke dies. He sells his textbooks, leaves the university without a degree, and signs on as an ordinary seaman aboard the sealer Magdalena. He takes his mate's papers two years after that. He is twenty-one.
suggested_refs: Franklin's published narratives, which Amundsen credited with setting the course of his life

stops.name: Hardangervidda: the plateau crossed on skis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The crossings are standard in the Fram Museum and MiA biographical chronologies but the dating varies from one retelling to the next; the file places the stop in the early 1890s with month and day defaulted. The pin is the plateau, not a route.
stops.campa: He crosses the high plateau on skis in winter, once failing badly enough that the attempt nearly kills him and once getting through with his brother Leon. Cold, hunger, sleeping rough, hauling a load a long way in bad light: he treats these as skills a man acquires by repetition, the way a mate acquires navigation, and he acquires them years before he has any expedition to spend them on. He is in his early twenties and has commanded nothing. The dating of the crossings differs from one account to the next.
suggested_refs: The Hardangervidda winter route, training ground of the Norwegian ski tradition Amundsen came out of

segments.name: Belgica: the First Winter in the Ice

stops.name: Antwerp: first mate of the Belgica
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1897 (Britannica; Fram Museum, 'the-belgica-expedition-1897-1899'); the pin is the ship's registered departure port and the month is given as August in the Fram Museum account, the day not fixed.
stops.campa: He ships out of Antwerp as first mate aboard Belgica, under the Belgian Adrien de Gerlache, in a crew drawn from several countries and including an American surgeon from Brooklyn named Frederick Cook. Amundsen is twenty-five and holds a mate's ticket. He has seen sealing ice off Norway and nothing at all like what he is sailing toward. The expedition means to survey the Antarctic coast and be clear of it before the season closes, and it carries no proper equipment for a winter in the pack.
suggested_refs: Amundsen's Belgica diary, published in a scholarly edition in 1999

stops.name: Bellingshausen Sea: beset, and the polar night
stops.date_confidence: the besetment and the winter drift of 1898 are attested (Fram Museum; Wikipedia, 'Roald Amundsen'); the exact date of besetment is not fixed in this pass and March is used to place the stop at the start of the drift. The pin is an approximate position in the drifting pack, which had no fixed location.
stops.campa: The pack takes the ship in March and does not let go. Belgica drifts through the polar night, the first vessel ever to winter in Antarctic waters, and does it by accident. One man dies, others break down in the dark, and scurvy comes into the ship. Cook and Amundsen shoot seal and penguin and force the fresh meat on a crew that does not want it, and the sick recover. Amundsen is twenty-six. He keeps his diary through the whole drift, and the drift lasts more than a year.
stops.quote: Frederick A. Cook, of Brooklyn, was surgeon to the expedition -- beloved and respected by all.
stops.quote_source: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole, vol. 1, trans. A. G. Chater (Project Gutenberg #4229)
suggested_refs: The Belgica's winter drift, first wintering in Antarctic waters

stops.name: Bellingshausen Sea: the channel cut out to open water
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1899 (Fram Museum chronology); month and day not fixed in this pass. Same approximate pack-ice pin as the besetment stop. Amundsen's later public defence of Cook is standard biography, not documented from a single citable letter in this pass.
stops.campa: A year in the ice and the ship is still held. The crew saws and blasts a channel out toward open water, working at a labour nobody has attempted before, and Belgica comes free. Cook's part in getting them out is large, and Amundsen never afterwards forgets it. Years later, when Cook is disgraced over his North Pole claim and dropped by respectable geographical society, Amundsen goes on defending him in print and in person, at real cost to his own standing among the men who had ruled on the question.
stops.quote: Upright, honourable, capable, and conscientious in the extreme -- such is the memory we retain of Frederick A. Cook from those days.
stops.quote_source: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole, vol. 1, trans. A. G. Chater (Project Gutenberg #4229)
suggested_refs: Cook's 1908 North Pole claim and the controversy that followed it

stops.name: Kristiania harbour: the Gjoa slips out at night
stops.date_confidence: departure date attested (Britannica; Wikipedia). The ship's dimensions are corrected here: the pool's '47-foot sloop' conflated length with tonnage, and Gjoa measured about 70 by 20 feet at 47 net register tons, built 1872, bought 28 March 1901 (Wikipedia, 'Gjoa'). The Hamburg magnetic training under Georg von Neumayer is a reconstruction and is carried in this campa rather than given a stop.
stops.campa: He buys the Gjoa in March 1901, a sloop of forty-seven register tons built in 1872, shoal enough to work water no naval vessel would risk. He studies geomagnetism in Hamburg under Georg von Neumayer, because the Northwest Passage on its own will not raise money and a magnetic programme at the North Magnetic Pole will. On the night of the sixteenth of June 1903, with a creditor threatening to seize the ship, seven men take her quietly out of Kristiania in the rain. The debt is documented. The midnight escape is his own telling.
suggested_refs: The Gjoa, 70 by 20 feet, 47 net register tonnage, built 1872, now at the Fram Museum, Oslo

stops.name: Beechey Island: Franklin's beach
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1903 (Fram Museum, Gjoa expedition itinerary); month given as summer, day not fixed, defaulted to 01. The twenty sled dogs taken aboard at Godhavn, Greenland (69.2455, -53.5325) belong to the same summer and are carried in this campa, Godhavn having no stop of its own.
stops.campa: Gjoa works up through Baffin Bay, takes twenty sled dogs aboard at Godhavn on the Greenland coast, and comes to Beechey Island, where Sir John Franklin's expedition wintered in 1845 before it went south into the ice and was never seen whole again. Amundsen has said that Franklin's narrative, read as a boy in Kristiania, was what decided him. He works his magnetic instruments here and then turns the ship down Peel Sound, the water Franklin took. Three graves stand above the beach.
suggested_refs: The three Franklin graves on Beechey Island, and Franklin's own published narratives

stops.name: Gjoa Haven, King William Island: the harbour with the bar across its mouth
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica chronology; Fram Museum itinerary). The Netsilik name Uqsuqtuuq is given in the Fram Museum and University of Oslo Historical Museum material; the file does not translate it, no verified gloss having been reached in this pass.
stops.campa: On the ninth of September, feeling south along King William Island through water shallow enough to have wrecked better ships, the crew finds a pocket of deep water on the south-east coast with a bar across its mouth. They put the ship inside it and let her freeze in. The magnetic observatory goes up ashore, huts of packing cases and snow, and the instruments begin their run. They will be here two full winters. The Netsilik name for the place is Uqsuqtuuq; the town that grows around the harbour will take the ship's name instead.
suggested_refs: The magnetic observatory at Gjoa Haven and its two-year run of observations

stops.name: Gjoa Haven: what the Netsilik teach them
stops.date_confidence: sustained contact from late October 1903 through August 1905 is attested (Fram Museum itinerary; University of Oslo Historical Museum, 'the Netsilik meet Amundsen'). The stop is dated 1904-01-01 to sit inside the two winters; no single date applies to a two-year relationship.
stops.campa: From late October 1903 the Netsilik come in to the ship, and for two years the two peoples live within sight of each other, trading, visiting, arguing, sitting in each other's houses. Amundsen sets his men to learn: how caribou skin is cut and sewn loose so that sweat does not freeze into it, how a snow house is raised in an hour, how dogs are driven and fed and worked and when they are not, how to hunt what is actually here. He writes it all down. The clothing that will bring five men back alive from the South Pole is Netsilik clothing, learned in this harbour.
suggested_refs: University of Oslo Historical Museum, 'the Netsilik meet Amundsen', and the Netsilik ethnographic collection Amundsen brought home

stops.name: Cape Colborne: the passage joined
stops.date_confidence: date attested (Britannica; Fram Museum itinerary). COORDINATES CORRECTED: the pool gave 70.45, -116.75, which sits in Amundsen Gulf, hundreds of kilometres ahead of where the ship was four days out of Gjoa Haven. GeoNames places Cape Colborne, Nunavut at 68.9647, -105.2411, at the approach to Cambridge Bay, which is the water charted from the west by Collinson. The file uses the GeoNames position.
stops.campa: Two years in the harbour, then west again through Simpson Strait, sounding ahead in water shallow enough to touch. On the seventeenth of August 1905 Gjoa enters sea that has already been charted from the Pacific side, and the Northwest Passage is joined in a single hull for the first time. Three centuries of Admiralty expeditions, lost ships, and eaten crews end here with a Norwegian sloop of forty-seven tons and seven men aboard her. Ice closes ahead of them within weeks and the voyage is not over.
suggested_refs: Collinson's charts of the western approaches, the water Gjoa entered on 17 August 1905

stops.name: Eagle, Alaska: the telegram out of the Yukon
stops.date_confidence: the overland dog journey to the telegraph station at Eagle is attested (Fram Museum itinerary) and belongs to the winter of 1905-1906; the exact date is not fixed in this pass and 5 December is used to place the stop inside that winter. Treat the day as a placement, not a record.
stops.campa: Frozen in at King Point near Herschel Island for a third winter, Amundsen takes a dog team and goes overland for the nearest telegraph, the army station at Eagle on the Yukon. He sends out the first word that the Northwest Passage has been sailed, waits through the winter for the answers, and drives back. Months of it, in the dark, over a route he has never travelled, with a team he has been driving since Gjoa Haven. He is back aboard at King Point in the spring, and the ship is still frozen in.
suggested_refs: The United States Army signal-corps telegraph station at Eagle, Alaska

stops.name: King Point, Yukon: Gustav Juel Wiik in the observatory
stops.date_confidence: attested (Fram Museum chronology). The pin is King Point, near Herschel Island, given to four decimals from the pool without independent survey.
stops.campa: Gustav Juel Wiik, the expedition's magnetic observer, the man who has run the instruments through two winters at Gjoa Haven, falls ill through the third winter at King Point and dies on the first of April 1906. He is the only man the expedition loses in three years, and he dies within one summer's sailing of Nome and the telegraph and the doctors. The others bury him beside the observatory they had built for the instruments. Amundsen goes on with the voyage west. The grave is still at King Point.
suggested_refs: Wiik's grave at the King Point magnetic observatory

stops.name: Nome, Alaska: the passage completed
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Fram Museum itinerary). Gjoa's later history is corrected from the pool: she went on display in Golden Gate Park in 1909, not 1906, and stood there until 1972 (Wikipedia, 'Gjoa'). No San Francisco stop is written, Amundsen's own presence at the donation not being established in this pass.
stops.campa: Gjoa comes into Nome on the last day of August 1906 with her flags up. The Northwest Passage has been sailed in one ship, the North Magnetic Pole has been located afresh, and three winters of magnetic records are in her hold. Amundsen is thirty-four and famous in every country that reads a newspaper. He is also in debt, and will be for the rest of his life. The ship never goes home: she is given away in San Francisco and stands in Golden Gate Park, weathering, until 1972.
suggested_refs: The Gjoa's outdoor display in Golden Gate Park, 1909-1972, and Erik Krag's campaign to bring her back to Norway

stops.name: Kristiania: Nansen gives up the Fram
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1908 (Fram Museum chronology); day not fixed and defaulted to 01. The pin is central Oslo, used throughout this file for Kristiania events without a fixed address.
stops.campa: He announces the next expedition in November 1908. Nansen's Fram, the strongest wooden ship afloat, is to be taken north through the Bering Strait and frozen deliberately into the pack for a drift of years across the polar basin. Fridtjof Nansen, who had the ship built and who wanted this drift for himself, gives her up to him. Nansen leaves no written account of why he yields. The Storting votes the money and the King subscribes. Within the year Frederick Cook and Robert Peary will both claim the North Pole.
suggested_refs: Nansen's Fram, built for the 1893-1896 drift, lent on to Amundsen in 1908

stops.name: Bunnefjord: the Fram leaves Norway with a false destination
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Roald Amundsen': the Fram left Norway on 3 June 1910). PLACE CORRECTED: the pool attached this date to Kristiansand; the June departure was from the Kristiania and Bundefjord area, and the Kristiansand departure was 9 August 1910. The pin is Amundsen's own house at Svartskog on the Bunnefjord, off which the ship was fitted out; it is a placement, not a documented mooring position.
stops.campa: Fram leaves Norwegian water on the third of June 1910, cleared for the Arctic Ocean by way of Cape Horn and the Bering Strait. Below her decks is a prefabricated hut, and sledging gear for a journey nobody aboard has been told about. Amundsen has known since the previous autumn that he is going south instead. Two men know it with him: his brother Leon, and Thorvald Nilsen, who commands the ship. Nansen, who lent the vessel, is not one of them, and neither is the Storting that voted the money.
suggested_refs: Uranienborg at Svartskog, Amundsen's house on the Bunnefjord, now a museum

stops.name: Kristiansand: ninety-seven dogs come aboard
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Amundsen's South Pole expedition': departure from Kristiansand after the trial cruise and final loading, 9 August 1910). Same harbour pin as the 1886 stop for the father's death; the two events share the town, not a documented spot in it.
stops.campa: Fram lies at Kristiansand through the summer, refitting and loading after a trial cruise in the North Atlantic, and here the Greenland dogs come aboard, ninety-seven of them, chained along the deck. She sails on the ninth of August 1910 with Leon Amundsen aboard as far as Madeira. The crew still believe they are bound around Cape Horn for the Bering Strait and five years in the ice. Twenty-four years earlier this harbour had taken his father. The son goes out past the same headland at thirty-eight.
suggested_refs: The ninety-seven Greenland dogs shipped at Kristiansand, ancestors of the Framheim teams

stops.name: Funchal, Madeira: the crew is told where it is going
stops.date_confidence: DATE CORRECTED: the pool gave 19 September 1910; Fram reached Funchal on 6 September and Amundsen told the crew on 9 September (Wikipedia, 'Amundsen's South Pole expedition'). The telegram to Scott, 'Beg to inform you Fram proceeding Antarctic', is quoted in the same source.
stops.campa: At Funchal the ship takes on water and fruit. On the ninth of September Amundsen has all hands mustered on deck, unrolls a chart of the Ross Sea, and tells them that they are going to the South Pole; then he asks each man in turn whether he will come. Every one of them says yes. Leon Amundsen goes ashore with the letters, among them a telegram for Robert Falcon Scott in Australia: Beg to inform you Fram proceeding Antarctic. Then the ship stands south and touches no port for four months.
stops.quote: Scott's plan and equipment were so widely different from my own that I regarded the telegram that I sent him later, with the information that we were bound for the Antarctic regions, rather as a mark of courtesy than as a communication which might cause him to alter his programme in the slightest degree.
stops.quote_source: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole, vol. 1, trans. A. G. Chater (Project Gutenberg #4229)
suggested_refs: The telegram to Scott sent from Funchal, September 1910

stops.name: Bay of Whales, Ross Ice Shelf: Framheim on floating ice
stops.date_confidence: arrival 14 January 1911 and completion of the hut 28 January are attested (Wikipedia, 'Roald Amundsen'; Fram Museum). The coordinates are approximate: the Bay of Whales ice front has since calved away and Framheim's platform no longer exists.
stops.campa: Fram pushes into the Bay of Whales on the fourteenth of January and lies against the ice front, further south than any ship has yet been laid alongside anything. The shore party runs up the hut in a fortnight, timber cut and numbered in Norway, and calls it Framheim. It stands on floating shelf ice some ninety-six kilometres nearer the Pole than the British base on Ross Island, and the chance that the whole shelf calves off and takes the hut with it is a risk Amundsen has weighed and accepted. By autumn there are more than a hundred dogs on the ice.
suggested_refs: Framheim, the Bay of Whales base, and the depot line laid to 82 degrees south in the autumn of 1911

stops.name: Ross Ice Shelf: the false start, and Johansen speaks
stops.date_confidence: attested to 8 September 1911 (Fram Museum chronology). The stop is placed at the Framheim pin because the party turned back to the base; the furthest point of the aborted start is not fixed in this pass.
stops.campa: He starts too early. On the eighth of September eight men go out onto the Barrier with the temperature falling past fifty below, and the dogs cannot work in it. The party turns and runs for home strung out over miles of ice, every sledge for itself, two men left behind in the dark to come in the next day frostbitten. Hjalmar Johansen, who crossed the polar ice with Nansen and outranks every man present in experience, says out loud in front of the others what he thinks of a leader who abandons his own rear. Amundsen does not answer him that day.
suggested_refs: Hjalmar Johansen's Arctic record with Nansen, 1893-1896, and his removal from the polar party

stops.name: Framheim: five men, four sledges, fifty-two dogs
stops.date_confidence: attested (Fram Museum chronology). Johansen's later fate after his removal is not carried here, no verified account of it having been reached in this pass.
stops.campa: Five men go out on the nineteenth of October: Amundsen, Olav Bjaaland, Helmer Hanssen, Sverre Hassel, Oscar Wisting, with four sledges and fifty-two dogs. Hjalmar Johansen is not among them. After the quarrel over the false start he has been struck off the polar party and sent on a side journey under a younger man, which ends his standing in the expedition. Everything on the sledges has been weighed and argued over through the winter. Depots stand ready ahead at eighty, eighty-one and eighty-two degrees south.
suggested_refs: The autumn depot line at 80, 81 and 82 degrees south, laid in February and March 1911

stops.name: The Butcher's Shop, top of the Axel Heiberg Glacier: the dogs are killed
stops.date_confidence: CORRECTED from the pool: the pool put the Butcher's Shop at -85.667 and said ten dogs were killed. Wikipedia's expedition article places the camp at 85 degrees 36 minutes south, which is about -85.60, and records 27 dogs killed with 18 going on; other accounts give 24, which is also Amundsen's own figure in The South Pole. The contradiction is left standing. The longitude is approximate.
stops.campa: The Barrier ends against mountains nobody has mapped. They find a glacier running up to the plateau in one long ramp, name it for the patron Axel Heiberg, and drive the dogs up three thousand metres in four days. At the top the plan comes due. The dogs that hauled the sledges up the glacier are shot, butchered, and fed to the dogs that will go on, and the men eat them too, counting the meat into the ration as carefully as they counted the biscuit. Accounts differ on whether twenty-four or twenty-seven die here. The camp is called the Butcher's Shop.
stops.quote: twenty-four of our brave companions and faithful helpers were marked out for death.
stops.quote_source: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole, vol. 2, trans. A. G. Chater (Project Gutenberg #3415)
suggested_refs: The Axel Heiberg Glacier, named for the Norwegian patron who financed the expedition
sources: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole, vol. 2 (Project Gutenberg #3415)

stops.name: The South Pole: the flag planted by five hands
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Wikipedia; Fram Museum). Some secondary sources historically printed 15 December through date-line confusion. The pin is the geographic pole itself, the same 0.0 longitude used for the North Pole elsewhere in the atlas.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of December the sledgemeters agree and the drivers stop. Five men take the flagstaff together, all five hands on the shaft, and set the Norwegian flag in the snow at ninety degrees south. They spend three days boxing the position with observations to be certain of it, name the plateau for King Haakon VII, and leave a tent with a letter for the King and a second letter addressed to Robert Falcon Scott, to be carried out by whoever comes next. The camp is called Polheim. Then they turn north, which from here is every direction there is.
stops.quote: We all assembled about the Norwegian flag -- a handsome silken flag -- which we took and planted all together
stops.quote_source: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole, vol. 1, 'The First Account', trans. A. G. Chater (Project Gutenberg #4229)
suggested_refs: Polheim: the tent, the King Haakon VII letter, and the letter left for Scott
Ernest Shackleton's own 1921 account, which dates the last great object of Antarctic travel from this fortnight
sources: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole, vol. 1 (Project Gutenberg #4229)

stops.name: Framheim: ninety-nine days, eleven dogs, five men
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Roald Amundsen'). DISTANCE CORRECTED: the pool gave roughly 3,000 km; the expedition article gives the round trip as approximately 1,860 nautical miles, about 3,440 km. Eleven dogs on two sledges and the 99-day duration are attested.
stops.campa: They come back in on the twenty-fifth of January 1912, ninety-nine days out, eleven dogs left on two sledges, all five men alive and none of them thinner than when they started. The round journey measures about eighteen hundred and sixty nautical miles. There is no crowd, no telegraph within thousands of miles, no other human being on the continent who knows: only the hut, the cook who wintered in it, and the sea ice going out. Fram comes in to the Barrier a few days later and takes the shore party off.
stops.quote: The distance from our winter quarters to the Pole was about 870 English miles, so that we had covered on an average 15 1/2 miles a day.
stops.quote_source: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole, vol. 1, 'The First Account', trans. A. G. Chater (Project Gutenberg #4229)
suggested_refs: Amundsen's own account of the return march in The South Pole, vol. 2
sources: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole (Project Gutenberg #4229)

stops.name: Hobart, Tasmania: the news goes out by cable
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Fram Museum). Scott's arrival at the Pole on 17 January 1912 and the deaths of his party on the return are attested in the general polar record; the news of them did not reach the world until 1913, which is carried at the Philadelphia stop.
stops.campa: Fram comes into Hobart on the seventh of March 1912 and Amundsen goes ashore to the telegraph office to send the news out himself, to the King first and then to the newspaper that has bought the exclusive rights to it. Within a day every capital in the world has it. He is thirty-nine. The lecture tours begin within the year and do not stop. Scott's party, five weeks behind him at the Pole and unheard from since, is at this hour somewhere on the Barrier, walking north.
suggested_refs: The Hobart telegraph office, from which the South Pole news was filed on 7 March 1912

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the patron on the River Plate
stops.date_confidence: Fram's arrival at Buenos Aires on 25 May 1912 is attested (Fram Museum, 'the-polar-ship-fram'). Whether Amundsen himself was aboard or ashore in Buenos Aires was not established in this pass; the stop is placed on the ship's movement and on his patron's presence there. Don Pedro Christophersen's patronage is a reconstruction, and the mountain named for him is not verified in this pass. The pin is the canonical Buenos Aires anchor used across the atlas, not the geography lens's -58.3705. CORRECTED: Fram never reached San Francisco; she waited at Colon, was refused the canal transit, returned to Buenos Aires, and went home to Horten on 16 July 1914.
stops.campa: Fram works up to Buenos Aires on the twenty-fifth of May 1912, out of money and needing a refit before any Arctic drift can begin. What keeps her afloat is a Norwegian who never sees the ice: Don Pedro Christophersen, a shipowner of the River Plate, who provisions and fuels the expedition out of his own pocket and will intervene again years later when Amundsen goes bankrupt. The Panama Canal is not finished. Fram waits at Colon, is turned back, comes here again, and finally goes home to Norway without ever entering the Arctic Ocean at all.
suggested_refs: Don Pedro Christophersen's provisioning of the third Fram expedition, and the Norwegian shipping community of the River Plate

stops.name: Philadelphia: three explorers in one photograph
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1913 (Wikipedia, 'Roald Amundsen'); day not fixed and defaulted to 01. News of Scott's death reached the world in February 1913 and is carried in this campa. Shackleton's own later statement about Amundsen is cited in the sources; it belongs to Shackleton's file as his own words.
stops.campa: On the American lecture circuit he sits for a photograph in Philadelphia with Ernest Shackleton on one side and Robert Peary on the other. Shackleton turned back ninety-seven miles short of the Pole four years before. Peary's North Pole claim of that same year is what had sent the Norwegian south. The three of them hold still for the camera in an American city, in the middle of a paying tour. The next month the world learns that Scott and four men died on the Barrier the previous March.
suggested_refs: Shackleton's 1921 account, which names Amundsen's conquest of the Pole as the reason the trans-Antarctic crossing became the one great object left

stops.name: Vollen, Asker: a ship built to be squeezed out of the ice
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1917 (Fram Museum); day not fixed. COORDINATES CORRECTED: the pool's geography lens gave 59.8333, 10.45, about five kilometres north of the village and inconsistent with its own afterlife entry; the file uses 59.7975, 10.4508, the same Vollen pin as Maud's 2018 return.
stops.campa: He orders a new ship from Christian Jensen's yard at Vollen on the Oslofjord, built to the Fram principle and rounder still: a hull the ice cannot grip, that is lifted instead of crushed. She costs more than he has. Queen Maud gives her name, and the ship goes down the ways in June 1917 into a Europe at war. The plan is the old one, the plan the South Pole interrupted: in along the Siberian coast, then freeze into the pack east of the New Siberian Islands and drift with it across the top of the world.
suggested_refs: Christian Jensen's yard at Vollen, and Maud's rounded hull after the Fram principle

stops.name: Vardo: the last Norwegian harbour
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Roald Amundsen'; Fram Museum). Crew given as nine men, later ten.
stops.campa: Maud clears Vardo on the eighteenth of July 1918, the last Norwegian harbour before the Russian Arctic, with nine men aboard and Harald Ulrik Sverdrup in charge of the science. Amundsen is forty-six. The Northeast Passage is the road and not the object; he means to work east past the New Siberian Islands and let the ice take the ship north. Sverdrup's programme covers oceanography, meteorology and magnetism, and it is written to run for as long as the ship is out.
suggested_refs: Harald Ulrik Sverdrup's scientific programme aboard Maud, 1918-1925

stops.name: Cape Chelyuskin: the arm, the bear, and the gas
stops.date_confidence: the carbon-monoxide poisoning of 10 December 1918 is given by the Fram Museum, which states that it left his health permanently impaired; the broken arm and the polar-bear mauling are from the same account and are tagged as institutional narrative rather than independently documented. The pin is Cape Chelyuskin; Maud lay east of it.
stops.campa: The ice stops Maud east of Cape Chelyuskin, the northernmost point of the Eurasian mainland, and holds her the better part of a year. In that winter Amundsen falls through new ice and breaks his arm in two places; a polar bear comes at him and mauls him before it is driven off; and on the tenth of December, working in the magnetic observatory, he is poisoned by carbon monoxide. The Fram Museum's account holds that his health never comes back from that winter, and nothing in the years after it contradicts the claim.
suggested_refs: The Maud expedition's magnetic observatory on the Taimyr coast

stops.name: Dikson: Tessem and Knudsen do not arrive
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The disappearance is attested in the Fram Museum material to 1919; the month is not fixed in this pass and is defaulted to 01. The pin is the destination, Port Dikson; neither the route nor the place of death is established, which is the point of the stop.
stops.campa: Peter Tessem and Paul Knudsen leave the ship to carry the expedition's records and mail overland to the telegraph station at Dikson, a long coastal march with dogs along the Taimyr shore. Neither man arrives. Search parties in the following years find a campsite, a cache, and human remains, and never establish what happened or in what order it happened. The errand is the delivery of paperwork. Which of the two dies first, and whether either one knows it, the searches never settle.
suggested_refs: The Soviet searches for Tessem and Knudsen along the Taimyr coast in the 1920s

stops.name: Nome, Alaska: both passages, one man
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Roald Amundsen'; Fram Museum). Third full navigation of the route after Nordenskiold's Vega (1878-1879) and the Russian Taymyr and Vaygach (1914-1915). The Seattle refit of 1921 is carried in this campa and has no stop of its own.
stops.campa: Maud comes into Nome on the twenty-eighth of July 1920 having sailed the Northeast Passage, the third ship ever to do it, after Nordenskiold's Vega and the Russian icebreakers Taymyr and Vaygach. No other man has sailed both passages. Measured against what he came to do it is a failure all the same: two years gone and the drift has not begun. Several of the crew leave at Nome and do not come back. The ship goes down to Seattle for repairs, and her owner spends the winter reading about aircraft.
suggested_refs: Nordenskiold's Vega, 1878-1879, and the Russian icebreakers Taymyr and Vaygach, 1914-1915

stops.name: Long Island, New York: the Junkers that does not reach Seattle
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1922 crash in Pennsylvania during a New York to Seattle flight with Oskar Omdal is from the Fram Museum and MiA aviation chronology; the exact departure field in the New York area is not confirmed, and the month is not fixed and is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He buys Junkers monoplanes with money he does not have and sets out to fly one of them from New York to Seattle with Oskar Omdal, a Norwegian naval pilot, as preparation for crossing the Arctic Ocean by air. The machine comes down in Pennsylvania. The second has to go west by rail. The aircraft of 1922 will not lift the fuel that a transpolar flight demands, and the man betting his name on them is fifty years old and borrowing against lecture fees he has not yet earned. He buys more aircraft.
suggested_refs: The MiA aircraft chronology for the 1922-1925 aviation attempts
sources: Roald Amundsen's House / MiA aircraft chronology

stops.name: Wainwright, Alaska: the base for a flight that is not made
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1923 (Fram Museum and MiA aviation chronology); month not fixed and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: A base goes up near Wainwright on the Alaskan coast north of the Bering Strait, and the plan is to fly from here across the pole to Spitsbergen: two men, one engine, and no landing ground for two thousand kilometres. The aircraft is damaged before the attempt can be made. Amundsen goes south again with nothing to show. The newspapers that paid in advance for the story begin asking after their money, and the house at Svartskog is already mortgaged.
suggested_refs: The Wainwright base of 1923 and the abandoned transpolar flight
sources: Roald Amundsen's House / MiA aviation chronology

stops.name: Uranienborg, Svartskog: the bankruptcy, and the two girls sent east
stops.date_confidence: the bankruptcy is recorded to September 1924 in the MiA/Uranienborg archive material; no criminal or judicial finding against Leon Amundsen or Haakon Hammer is established in the archival record, and the blame is Amundsen's own. CORRECTED: the adopted girl was Kakonita, called Nita, not 'Nita Kakot'; she and Camilla were sent to be cared for by Camilla's father in eastern Russia, and Camilla's father was a foreign trader, so the pool's 'two Chukchi girls' oversimplifies. The 1924 dating of their departure follows the bankruptcy year and inherits its uncertainty.
stops.campa: The bankruptcy is entered in September 1924. He blames his brother Leon, who has handled his money for twenty years, and the businessman Haakon Hammer; the brothers never speak again, and no court ever finds against either man. The house at Svartskog goes with everything else, until friends buy it back for his lifetime use. In the same collapse the two children he brought home from the Siberian coast, the four-year-old Kakonita whom he had adopted and her companion Camilla, are put aboard a ship east to be raised by Camilla's father. He does not see them again.
suggested_refs: The Uranienborg bankruptcy papers in the MiA archive
Espen Ytreberg's work on Kakonita and Camilla
sources: Roald Amundsen's House / MiA (amundsen.mia.no) bankruptcy documentation

segments.name: The Flying Boats and the Airship

stops.name: Ny-Alesund, Svalbard: N 24 and N 25 lift off the water
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Fram Museum, 'the-n24-n25-flight-towards-the-north-pole-1925'). Six men in two Dornier Wal flying boats, with Lincoln Ellsworth financing and Hjalmar Riiser-Larsen and Leif Dietrichson among the pilots.
stops.campa: Two Dornier Wal flying boats, N 24 and N 25, come off the water at Kings Bay on the twenty-first of May 1925 carrying six men, among them the American Lincoln Ellsworth, who has paid for them, and the pilots Hjalmar Riiser-Larsen and Leif Dietrichson. There is fuel for the Pole and back and nothing spare. No aircraft has been to that latitude, and there is no ground to come down on for a thousand kilometres in any direction. They intend to land at the Pole, take soundings through the ice, and come home the same way.
suggested_refs: The Dornier Wal flying boats N 24 and N 25, and Lincoln Ellsworth's financing of the 1925 flight

stops.name: Eighty-seven degrees forty-three minutes north: a runway cut in moving ice
stops.date_confidence: DATES CORRECTED. The pool attributed a 22 May landing and a 6 June takeoff to Britannica; the Fram Museum's N24/N25 page gives the forced landing on 21 May 1925, the same day they left, after more than eight hours of flight, and the takeoff on 15 June 1925, about three and a half weeks later. A 6 June takeoff also contradicts the pool's own 'over three weeks'. The longitude of the landing is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: After more than eight hours the engines have drunk more than the arithmetic allowed and both machines put down in leads in the drifting pack at eighty-seven degrees forty-three minutes north. N 24 is finished. Six men, one usable aircraft, rations counted in weeks: for three and a half weeks they cut and stamp a runway out of pack ice that keeps opening and closing under them, with what tools the aircraft happened to carry. On the fifteenth of June the overloaded N 25 gets off the ice with all six aboard and comes down on open water off Svalbard, where a sealer takes them in.
suggested_refs: The abandoned N 24 on the pack ice at 87 degrees 43 minutes north

stops.name: The North Pole: the Norge overhead and three flags down
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Fram Museum, 'the-norge-flight-1926'). CORRECTED: the pool called Nobile the airship's commander. Nobile designed the airship and served as its pilot; Amundsen led the expedition (Wikipedia, 'Norge (airship)'). Financing was Ellsworth together with the Norsk Luftseiladsforening, not Ellsworth alone. The 11 May 1926 departure from Ny-Alesund at 09:55 is carried in this campa. The pin is the geographic pole, the same 90.0 / 0.0 used elsewhere in the atlas.
stops.campa: The airship Norge leaves the mast at Ny-Alesund on the eleventh of May 1926, designed and piloted by the Italian Umberto Nobile, paid for by Lincoln Ellsworth together with the Norwegian Aero Club, with Amundsen leading the expedition. In the early hours of the twelfth she comes over the Pole. The engines are throttled back and three flags go down onto the ice, Norwegian, American, Italian, dropped through a hatch from a slow airship onto a point that no undisputed traveller has yet stood on. Richard Byrd's claim of three days earlier is contested; this one is not.
suggested_refs: The Norge, designed by Umberto Nobile, and the contested Byrd flight of 9 May 1926

stops.name: Teller, Alaska: seventy-two hours across the Arctic Ocean
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Fram Museum, 'the-norge-flight-1926').
stops.campa: Fog, ice loading the envelope, gas-bag fabric torn and patched in flight: after roughly seventy-two hours in the air Norge comes down at Teller, a village on the Alaskan coast short of Nome. Europe to America over the pole: the first crossing of the Arctic Ocean by air and the first crossing of it by any means. Amundsen is fifty-three years old and has now been first at both ends of the earth. The crew climb out of the gondola into snow, and Norge is dismantled where she lies.
suggested_refs: The landing site at Teller, Alaska, 14 May 1926

stops.name: Oslo: the homecoming, and the book that settles scores
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the scale of the reception, which comes from Fram Museum narrative material; July 1926 with the day defaulted to 01. The publication of Mitt liv som polarforsker in 1927 and its attacks on Nobile are attested in the same source.
stops.campa: Oslo receives the Norge crew in July with crowds along the harbour, and the bankrupt of two years before is a national possession again. He says he is finished with expeditions. What he does instead is write. Mitt liv som polarforsker, My Life as an Explorer, comes out in 1927 with its scores settled in public, and its pages on Umberto Nobile are hard enough that Nobile answers in kind. By the spring of 1928 the two men who crossed the Arctic Ocean together in the same gondola are not on speaking terms.
suggested_refs: Mitt liv som polarforsker (My Life as an Explorer), 1927, and Nobile's replies

segments.name: The Latham and the Empty Sea

stops.name: Uranienborg, Svartskog: the debts cleared before he goes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Italia dates are CORRECTED from the pool: the airship reached the Pole on 24 May 1928 and crashed on 25 May near 81 degrees 14 minutes north, northeast of Nordaustlandet (Wikipedia, 'Italia (airship)'), not 23 May. The instruction to the lawyer, 'Make me a free man', is attributed in Fram Museum institutional history and was not verified against a letter or court record in this pass; the sale of part of the medal collection comes from the same material. June 1928 with the day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of May 1928 Nobile's new airship Italia strikes the ice north-east of Nordaustlandet on the way back from the Pole. Nine men are left alive on a floe with a tent dyed red and a radio, and the rescue becomes an international operation of six nations and a dozen aircraft. At Svartskog the man who has not spoken to Nobile in two years puts his own affairs in order. He offers himself to the search, and sells part of the medal collection to clear what is left of the debt. The instruction he gives his lawyer, which the Fram Museum carries and no document confirms, is: make me a free man.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Amundsen, instruction to his lawyer, 1928, in Fram Museum institutional history; not verified against a primary document
suggested_refs: The Red Tent camp on the ice north of Svalbard, and the Krassin rescue of 12 July 1928
sources: Roald Amundsen's House / MiA archive material

stops.name: Tromso: the Latham 47 takes off and is not heard again
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Wikipedia, 'Latham 47'). Radio contact was lost within hours of departure. The assessment of the aircraft as an untested prototype for the conditions comes from Karen May and George Lewis in Polar Record.
stops.campa: The aircraft waiting at Tromso is a Latham 47, a French naval flying boat, a prototype with few hours behind it and no experience of ice at all. Amundsen has never flown in the type. He goes aboard on the eighteenth of June 1928 with the pilot Rene Guilbaud, three other Frenchmen, and Leif Dietrichson, who was on the pack ice with him at eighty-seven degrees north three years before. They take off in the afternoon for Kings Bay. A few hours out the wireless operator sends a routine message, and after that there is nothing.
suggested_refs: Karen May and George Lewis, Polar Record, on the loss of Latham 47
The Latham 47.02, French naval prototype flying boat

stops.name: The coast off Troms: a float comes ashore
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Latham 47': the torn-off port float found off the coast of Troms, 31 August 1928). CONTRADICTION NOT RESOLVED: the pool's Fram Museum-derived chronology reads the recovered artifacts as indicating a crash south of Bjornoya, while the Latham 47 article draws no conclusion at all and says the aircraft disappeared without a trace. Both float and fuel tank came ashore south of Bjornoya, off mainland Norway, which is consistent with drift and establishes no crash site. The file records no crash location. The pin is an approximate position on the Troms coast.
stops.campa: On the thirty-first of August a float torn from a flying boat is picked up off the Troms coast and identified as the port float of Latham 47.02. It is the first physical trace of the aircraft after ten weeks of searching. Norway calls off the search in September. What the float establishes is that the machine came down on water. Where it came down, and whether any of the six men were alive when it did, the float does not say, and no source that this research could reach says it either.
suggested_refs: The recovered port float of Latham 47.02, first physical trace of the aircraft
sources: Karen May and George Lewis, Polar Record, on the Latham 47 loss

stops.name: Haltenbanken: the last piece ever found
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1928 (Wikipedia, 'Latham 47'); day not fixed and defaulted to 01. The Royal Norwegian Navy's seabed searches with the unmanned submarine Hugin 1000 in 2004 and 2009, both of which found nothing, are attested in Wikipedia, 'Roald Amundsen', and are carried in this campa.
stops.campa: In October a large fuel tank, modified by hand for extra range, comes up on the fishing bank of Haltenbanken far to the south, off Trondelag. It is the last piece of Latham 47.02 ever recovered. No wreck, no bodies, no grave. The Royal Norwegian Navy will drag the seabed off Tromso with an unmanned submarine in 2004 and again in 2009, and find nothing belonging to the aircraft. Rene Guilbaud, Leif Dietrichson and three other Frenchmen went down with him. He was fifty-five.
suggested_refs: The Hugin 1000 seabed searches off Tromso, 2004 and 2009
The Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, named jointly for the two rivals in 1956
